summary: Defines how OAuth 2.0 clients can register themselves dynamically with an authorization server. The client sends metadata about itself and gets back a client identifier to use later.

plainLanguage.summary: Before an app can use an OAuth 2.0 server, it needs a client identifier and a few details about itself. This document lets the app send those details to the server over the network and get an identifier back, so nobody has to fill in a form by hand.

questions: what is oauth dynamic client registration

subtitle: How an OAuth 2.0 client asks an authorization server for its client identifier and details.

tldr.problem: An OAuth 2.0 client needs a client identifier and a set of details, such as its valid redirection URIs, before it can use an authorization server. Registering those by hand does not scale when many applications and many servers are involved.
tldr.mechanism: The client sends an HTTP POST with a JSON body of client metadata to the client registration endpoint, optionally with an initial access token and a signed software statement. The server answers with a client identifier, a client secret if the client is confidential, and the metadata it actually registered.
tldr.outcome: Clients and developers can register themselves with any number of servers automatically. The server must still treat the metadata as self-asserted unless a trusted software statement vouches for it.

today: RFC 7591 is a Proposed Standard published in July 2015. It has not been obsoleted or updated, so it remains the standard way for an OAuth 2.0 client to register itself with an authorization server over the network.

sections.title: Why Clients Need to Register
sections.content:
An OAuth 2.0 client needs specific information before it can use an authorization server, including a client identifier for that server. This document describes how a client obtains that information by registering itself with the server over the network.

Registration also lets the client present metadata about itself, such as the set of valid redirection URIs. That metadata can be sent in a self-asserted fashion or as a software statement, a bundle of claims that is digitally signed or protected with a Message Authentication Code (MAC). In the case of a software statement, the issuer is vouching for the validity of the data about the client.

Traditionally, registration of a client with an authorization server is performed manually. The mechanisms here can be used either for a client to register itself with authorization servers or for a client developer to register the client programmatically. Several applications using OAuth 2.0 had already developed their own registration mechanisms. This specification generalizes the mechanisms defined by OpenID Connect Dynamic Client Registration 1.0 and used by the User-Managed Access profile of OAuth 2.0 in a way compatible with both, while applying to a wider set of OAuth 2.0 use cases.
sections.plainLanguage: An app that uses OAuth 2.0 needs an identifier for the server it will talk to. This document lets the app ask the server for one over the network, instead of a person filling in a form. The app can also send details about itself, such as where the server should send the user back to.

sections.title: The Registration Flow
sections.content:
The flow has four steps. First, optionally, the client or developer is issued an initial access token that gives access to the client registration endpoint; how that token is issued is out of scope. Second, optionally, the client or developer is issued a software statement for use with the endpoint, and again how it is issued is out of scope.

Third, the client or developer calls the client registration endpoint with the client's desired registration metadata, optionally including the initial access token if the authorization server requires one. Fourth, the authorization server registers the client and returns the client's registered metadata, a client identifier that is unique at the server, and a set of client credentials such as a client secret, if one applies to this client. The figure in the RFC does not show error conditions.

The document also describes several configurations: registration that is open to anyone or restricted to authorized parties, registration with or without a software statement, registration by the client itself or by the developer, a client identifier per client instance or shared by all instances of the same software, and registration that keeps state at the server or is stateless.
sections.plainLanguage: The flow has four steps. The app may be given a token that allows it to register, and it may be given a signed note about the software. Then it posts its details to the registration endpoint, and the server replies with a client identifier, a secret if the app needs one, and the details it actually stored.

sections.title: Client Metadata
sections.content:
Registered clients have a set of metadata values associated with their client identifier, such as the list of valid redirection URIs or a display name. These values are used both as input to registration requests and as output in registration responses. The implementation and use of all client metadata fields is OPTIONAL unless stated otherwise, and all data member types are defined in terms of their JSON representations.

  • redirect_uris: an array of redirection URI strings for use in redirect-based flows such as the authorization code and implicit flows. Clients using flows with redirection MUST register their redirection URI values, and authorization servers that support dynamic registration for redirect-based flows MUST implement support for this value.
  • token_endpoint_auth_method: a string naming the requested authentication method for the token endpoint. The values defined here are none, for a public client that has no client secret, client_secret_post, and client_secret_basic. If unspecified or omitted, the default is client_secret_basic.
  • grant_types and response_types: arrays of the OAuth 2.0 grant types the client may use at the token endpoint, and the response types it may use at the authorization endpoint. If grant_types is omitted, the client will use only the authorization_code grant type; if response_types is omitted, only the code response type.
  • client_name, client_uri, logo_uri, tos_uri and policy_uri: a human-readable name to show the end-user, a web page about the client, a logo, the terms of service, and the privacy policy.
  • scope: a space-separated list of scope values the client can use when requesting access tokens. If omitted, the server MAY register the client with a default set of scopes.
  • contacts: an array of ways to contact the people responsible for the client, typically email addresses.
  • jwks_uri and jwks: the client's JSON Web Key Set, either as a URL to fetch or as the document itself. Use of jwks_uri is preferred because it makes key rotation easier, and the two parameters MUST NOT both be present in the same request or response.
  • software_id and software_version: an identifier for the client software and a version string for it. The software_id SHOULD stay the same across all instances and updates of the same software, unlike the client_id that the server issues.

The two arrays are related. A grant_types value that includes authorization_code implies a response_types value that includes code, and implicit implies token. A server supporting these fields SHOULD keep a client from registering itself into an inconsistent state, for example by returning an invalid_client_metadata error.

The authorization server MUST ignore any client metadata it does not understand, for instance by silently removing unknown metadata from the registration record, and it MAY reject requested values by replacing them with suitable defaults or by returning an error. Metadata can be sent directly in the body of a registration request or included as claims in a software statement, and a mixture of both is possible. If the same metadata name is present in both places and the software statement is trusted by the server, the claim in the software statement takes precedence.

Human-readable values may be given in several languages. BCP 47 language tags are added to metadata member names, delimited by a number sign character, so a client can send client_name#en and client_name#ja-Jpan-JP in the same request. If a human-readable field is sent without a language tag, the value MUST be used as is, with no assumption about its language, character set or script.
sections.plainLanguage: The details a client can send are called metadata. The important ones are the list of addresses the server may send the user back to, the way the client will prove itself at the token endpoint, the list of OAuth grants it wants, a name and a logo to show the user, and the client's public keys. The server must ignore fields it does not understand.

sections.title: Software Statements
sections.content:
A software statement is a JSON Web Token (JWT) that asserts metadata values about the client software as a bundle. When it is presented to the authorization server as part of a registration request, it MUST be digitally signed or MACed using JSON Web Signature (JWS) and MUST contain an iss (issuer) claim denoting the party attesting to the claims. It is RECOMMENDED that software statements be digitally signed using the RS256 signature algorithm, although particular applications MAY specify other algorithms. It is RECOMMENDED that a software statement carry the software_id claim, so that the server can correlate different instances of software using the same statement.

In some cases a statement is issued directly by the client developer, and in others by a third-party organization for the developer to use. In both cases the trust relationship the authorization server has with the issuer is intended to be an input to the evaluation of whether the registration request is accepted. The statement is typically distributed with all instances of a client application, and the means by which a client or developer obtains one are outside the scope of this specification.

The criteria by which an authorization server determines whether to trust and use the information in a software statement are outside the scope of this specification. In some cases an authorization server MAY accept a software statement value directly as a client identifier in an authorization request, without a prior dynamic client registration; the circumstances and the specific software statement characteristics required in that case are outside the scope as well.
sections.plainLanguage: A software statement is a signed token that carries the same details as a bundle. The signature lets the server check that the details really came from the software publisher, and that nobody changed them on the way. How the server decides which publishers to trust is left to the server.

sections.title: The Registration Endpoint and the Request
sections.content:
The client registration endpoint is an OAuth 2.0 endpoint defined in this document that is designed to allow a client to be registered with the authorization server. The means by which the URL for this endpoint is obtained are out of scope for this specification.

The endpoint MUST accept HTTP POST messages with request parameters encoded in the entity body using the application/json format, and it MUST be protected by a transport-layer security mechanism. It MAY be an OAuth 2.0 protected resource and it MAY accept an initial access token in the form of an OAuth 2.0 access token, to limit registration to only previously authorized parties. The method by which such a token is obtained is generally out of band and out of scope, as is the method by which the endpoint verifies it.

To support open registration and to facilitate wider interoperability, the endpoint SHOULD allow registration requests with no authorization. Such requests MAY be rate-limited or otherwise limited to prevent a denial-of-service attack on the client registration endpoint.

To register, the client or developer sends an HTTP POST to the client registration endpoint with a content type of application/json. The HTTP entity payload is a JSON document consisting of a JSON object with all requested client metadata values as top-level members of that object. The authorization server assigns the client a unique client identifier, optionally assigns a client secret, and associates the metadata in the request with the issued identifier. The server MAY provision default values for any items omitted from the client metadata. Client metadata values may also be provided inside a software statement, in which case they take precedence over plain JSON elements if the server supports the feature.
sections.plainLanguage: The registration endpoint takes an HTTP POST with a JSON body. It must be protected by TLS. To make registration widely available the server should accept requests with no token, but it may limit how often those come in.

sections.title: What the Server Returns
sections.content:
On a successful registration the server responds with an HTTP 201 Created status code and a body of type application/json. The response contains the client identifier and, if the client is a confidential client, the client secret, and it MAY contain additional fields from extensions to this specification.

  • client_id is REQUIRED. It SHOULD NOT be currently valid for any other registered client, though a server MAY issue the same identifier to multiple instances of a registered client at its discretion.
  • client_secret is OPTIONAL. If issued it MUST be unique for each client_id and SHOULD be unique for multiple instances of a client using the same identifier. Confidential clients use it to authenticate to the token endpoint.
  • client_id_issued_at is OPTIONAL and gives the time the identifier was issued, as the number of seconds from 1970-01-01T00:00:00Z measured in UTC until issuance.
  • client_secret_expires_at is REQUIRED if a secret is issued, giving the time the secret expires or 0 if it will not expire.

The server MUST return all registered metadata about the client, including any fields it provisioned itself, and it MAY reject or replace any of the requested values with suitable ones. The client can check the returned values to see whether the registration is sufficient for use and decide what to do next. If a software statement was used, its value MUST be returned unmodified under the software_statement member name, and the metadata taken from the statement MUST also be returned as top-level values, which may differ from the values requested.

When a registration error occurs, the server responds with an HTTP 400 status code, unless otherwise specified, with a content type of application/json and a JSON object describing the error. Two members are defined: error is REQUIRED and holds a single ASCII error code string, and error_description is OPTIONAL and holds human-readable ASCII text used for debugging. Other members MAY be included and MUST be ignored if they are not understood. The codes defined here are invalid_redirect_uri, invalid_client_metadata, invalid_software_statement and unapproved_software_statement.
sections.plainLanguage: On success the server replies with HTTP 201 and a JSON body that holds the client identifier, a secret if the client is confidential, and every metadata value that was stored. If something is wrong, it replies with HTTP 400 and an error code, such as invalid_redirect_uri or invalid_client_metadata.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Registration requests and responses carry clear-text credentials, so the authorization server MUST require a transport-layer security mechanism when sending requests to the registration endpoint. The server MUST support TLS 1.2 and MAY support additional mechanisms that meet its security requirements, and the client MUST perform a TLS/SSL server certificate check.

For clients that use redirect-based grant types such as authorization_code and implicit, authorization servers MUST require clients to register their redirection URI values. This helps mitigate attacks where rogue actors inject and impersonate a validly registered client and intercept its authorization code or tokens through an invalid redirection URI or an open redirector. To prevent hijacking of the return values of the redirection, registered redirection URI values MUST be one of: a remote web site protected by TLS, a web site hosted on the local machine using an HTTP URI such as http://localhost:8080/oauth_redirect, or a non-HTTP application-specific URL available only to the client application.

Unless used as a claim in a software statement, the authorization server MUST treat all client metadata as self-asserted. A rogue client might use the name and logo of a legitimate client, or its software identifier and software version, to associate itself with instances of that client. The server MUST take appropriate steps to mitigate this risk by looking at the entire registration request and client configuration. It could issue a warning if the domain of the logo does not match the domain of the redirection URIs, refuse registration requests from a known software identifier that ask for different redirection URIs or a different client URI, or present warning messages to end-users about dynamically registered clients, especially those recently registered or not previously trusted at the server.

With open client registration the server must be extremely careful with any URL the client provides that will be displayed to the user, such as logo_uri, tos_uri, client_uri and policy_uri. A rogue client could point the privacy policy at a drive-by download and entice the user to click it. The server SHOULD check that these URLs have the same host and scheme as the values in the array of redirect_uris and that they resolve to valid web pages, and SHOULD protect the user from malicious content hosted there, for instance by downloading the content, checking it against a malware scanner and blacklist filter, and looking for mixed secure and non-secure content. It can also warn the user that the links were provided by a third party and are not hosted by the server itself.

A software statement is still an item of metadata that the client asserts about itself, even though its contents are signed or MACed by the issuer, so presenting one is not enough in most cases to fully identify a piece of client software. The server MUST consider the full registration request, including the software statement, the initial access token and the JSON metadata, when deciding whether to honor it. If the server can infer that a registration duplicates an existing one, for example from the same software_id and software_version, it SHOULD treat the new registration as suspect and reject it. A server that issues the same client identifier to multiple instances must be very particular about the circumstances, and it SHOULD NOT issue the same client secret to multiple instances, or else the secret could be leaked and let malicious impostors impersonate a confidential client.
sections.plainLanguage: The server must use TLS, and it must check the addresses a client registers so that a fake client cannot hijack the reply that carries the user's permission. It must also treat the details a client sends as unverified claims, and be careful with any web address it will show the user.

sections.title: Privacy Considerations
sections.content:
The protocol deals almost exclusively with information about software and not people, so there are very few privacy concerns. The notable exception is the contacts field, which holds contact information for the developers or other parties responsible for the client software. Those values are intended to be displayed to end-users and are available to the administrators of the authorization server, so a developer may wish to give an address dedicated to client support rather than a personal or professional one, or a collective address so that support continues when the developer moves on.

Metadata such as the client name and software identifier is common across all instances of a piece of client software and therefore poses no privacy issues for end-users. Client identifiers, on the other hand, are often unique to a specific instance. For clients such as web sites used by many users this matters little, but for a native application installed on one end-user's device the identifier could be tracked during OAuth 2.0 transactions and tied to that one person. That tracking can happen whether or not the identifier is unique, by correlating the authenticated resource owner with the requesting client identifier.

Clients are forbidden from creating their own client identifier, because an individual client instance could then be tracked across multiple colluding authorization servers. Client identifiers are generally issued uniquely per registration request, even for the same instance of software, so an application could marginally improve its privacy by registering several times and appearing to be completely separate applications. That technique does incur a significant usability cost, because it requires multiple authorizations per resource owner, and is therefore unlikely to be used in practice.
sections.plainLanguage: The protocol mostly talks about software, not people, so privacy problems are rare. The one field that names people is the contact list. A client identifier can also be used to follow one person's app from one server to another, which is why the client is not allowed to choose its own identifier.

viz.caption: A NON-NORMATIVE REGISTRATION REQUEST FROM RFC 7591 SECTION 3.1

data.title: Registration request
data.code:
POST /register HTTP/1.1
Content-Type: application/json
Accept: application/json
Host: server.example.com

{
 "redirect_uris": [
   "https://client.example.org/callback",
   "https://client.example.org/callback2"],
 "client_name": "My Example Client",
 "token_endpoint_auth_method": "client_secret_basic",
 "logo_uri": "https://client.example.org/logo.png",
 "jwks_uri": "https://client.example.org/my_public_keys.jwks",
 "example_extension_parameter": "example_value"
}

viz.caption: THE REGISTRATION ERROR CODES DEFINED BY RFC 7591

items.label: Bad redirection URI
items.desc: The value of one or more redirection URIs is invalid.

items.label: Bad metadata
items.desc: The value of one of the client metadata fields is invalid and the server has rejected the request.

items.label: Bad statement
items.desc: The software statement presented is invalid.

items.label: Unapproved statement
items.desc: The software statement presented is not approved for use by this authorization server.
